newsitem.title: USA: Canada may step up wheat sales to US -US exporters.
newsitem.headline: Canada may step up wheat sales to US -US exporters.

text.p: As Canada's harvest gets into full swing this month the Canadian Wheat Board may be stepping up wheat exports to the United States, offering competitive prices to U.S. flour mills, U.S. export and mill sources said.

"U.S. wheat is still cheaper for domestic mills but we heard that the Canadian Wheat Board is offering wheat that is pretty close to being competitive to U.S. wheat, and they will get more aggressive as time goes on," one U.S. exporter said.
A rise in Canadian grain exports to the United States in 1993-94 sparked U.S. farmer protests, a war of words over free markets, and a one-year U.S. cap on Canadian wheat shipments.
The cap was lifted a year ago but U.S. officials have kept a sharp eye on Canadian exports, keeping the issue sensitive.
The Canadian Wheat Board, which has a monopoly on exports of Canadian prairie wheat and barley, declined comment.

"I will not comment on any of our sales activities. That is commercially sensitive information. We do not confirm or deny any rumor in sales activity," said Deanna Allen, the CWB's communications officer in Winnipeg.
As of July 1996, Canada had shipped 746,400 tonnes of wheat other than durum to the United States, below 1,205,900 tonnes a year earlier, the Canadian Grain Commission said.

The U.S. exporter said some CWB business is done every year to U.S. mills, but this year it may be more than normal because of Canada's large wheat crop. The exporter said he expects U.S. flour mills to eventually buy Canadian wheat although he did not believe they had bought anything yet.
"They (U.S. mills) are using this as leverage against the domestic stuff here to get a better price," he said.
A second U.S. exporter also heard rumors but had no confirmation.
"I am sure they (Canada) are certainly taking a look at the options," the exporter said.

"They have a good crop coming in and they are starting to scull around. They are going to figure out what our wheat is trading at and offer slightly below that. But it is nothing unusual that I have seen," the second exporter said.
A senior U.S. mill industry source, who also declined to be identified, said it was difficult to confirm negotiations between the CWB and U.S. mills because they are confidential.

"There is nothing ever published," he said. "What we are seeing are indications of a larger Canadian wheat crop this year and I believe that people are surmising that they will be more aggressive selling their wheat to U.S. mills."
"All of the studies we had in the past have shown that they do not undercut U.S. prices," the milling source said.
"They are basing their values off of U.S. markets and clearly U.S. mills would not buy the product if they did not think it was of value to them," he said.

"Basically, what we have is a North American market that is giving value to individual wheat shipments whether they be U.S. or Canada. I would not be surprised to see this happening," the milling source added.
Sources said with quality problems this year in the U.S. soft red winter wheat crop particularly, Canadian wheat would be valuable to blend if the price was right.
On the other hand, one Canadian exporter does not see Canada shipping more wheat than normal this year.
"We are quite active in that business and we have had much busier years than this one," he said. "Sounds like someone who is short the market and wants to scare some people," he said.
--Chicago Newsdesk 312-983-7305
